---
title: "Experiment 01 — Prisoner's Dilemma"
---

# Overview

Do LLM agents cooperate or defect when placed in a repeated strategic interaction — without being told what game they are playing?

This experiment sets up two teams of agents in a repeated two-choice environment. The agents are given neutral labels (**option_a** and **option_b**) and are never told the payoff structure is a prisoner's dilemma. The goal is to observe whether cooperation emerges, and how team discussion affects decision-making.

::: {.callout-note}
Source code and full results: **[github.com/1dzl0/agent-game](https://github.com/1dzl0/agent-game)**
:::

---

# Game Design

## Payoff Matrix

Each round, both teams independently choose option_a or option_b. Rewards are determined by the combination of both teams' choices.

|  | **Team B: option_a** | **Team B: option_b** |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| **Team A: option_a** | 3, 3 | 0, 5 |
| **Team A: option_b** | 5, 0 | 1, 1 |

This is the classic prisoner's dilemma structure:

- **Mutual cooperation** (A, A) → both score 3 — best joint outcome
- **Mutual defection** (B, B) → both score 1 — worst joint outcome
- **Unilateral defection** → defector scores 5, cooperator scores 0

Agents see only "option_a" and "option_b" in their prompts. The payoff values are revealed through the history of rounds, not upfront.

## Agent Architecture

Each team has multiple agents. Before each round, agents share private messages within their team, then each agent votes independently. The team's final action is determined by majority vote.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    GS[Game State\npublic history + scores] --> OA[Observation Builder]
    TH[Private Team History] --> OA

    OA --> D1[Agent 1\nDiscussion]
    OA --> D2[Agent 2\nDiscussion]

    D1 -->|private message| TV[Team Vote]
    D2 -->|private message| TV

    TV --> DA1[Agent 1\nDecision]
    TV --> DA2[Agent 2\nDecision]

    DA1 -->|vote| MV[Majority Vote]
    DA2 -->|vote| MV

    MV --> TA[Team Action]
    TA --> RM[Reward\nCalculation]
    RM --> GS
```

## What agents are told

Agents receive a prompt like this each round — no mention of game theory, prisoner's dilemma, or strategic naming:

```
You are team_alpha_agent_1, a participant in a repeated decision setting.
This is round 3 of 5.
Your team score: 6.

Public history:
Round 1: team_alpha selected option_a, team_beta selected option_a. team_alpha received 3 points, team_beta received 3 points.
Round 2: team_alpha selected option_a, team_beta selected option_a. team_alpha received 3 points, team_beta received 3 points.

Private team channel:
team_alpha_agent_1: ...
team_alpha_agent_2: ...

The available choices are option_a and option_b.
```

---

# Baseline Run

**Configuration:** 2 teams × 2 agents, 5 rounds, model: `gpt-4.1-nano`

## Round-by-Round Results

| Round | Team Alpha | Team Beta | Alpha +pts | Beta +pts | Joint |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 1 | option_a | option_a | 3 | 3 | 6 |
| 2 | option_a | option_a | 3 | 3 | 6 |
| 3 | option_a | option_a | 3 | 3 | 6 |
| 4 | option_a | option_a | 3 | 3 | 6 |
| 5 | option_a | option_a | 3 | 3 | 6 |

**Final scores:** Team Alpha 15, Team Beta 15 — Draw

**Cooperation rate:** 100% (10/10 decisions) · **Mutual cooperation:** 5/5 rounds · **Defections:** 0

## Agent Reasoning

A selection of private team messages showing how agents reasoned about their choices:

**Round 1 — Team Alpha (no history yet):**

> *"In round 1, since there's no prior history or signals, I'll choose option_a to start the iteration with a cooperative stance, assuming this may set a positive tone for future rounds."*

> *"Given the initial round and no prior signals, I suggest we choose option_a to promote cooperation early on. This might encourage a collaborative pattern for subsequent rounds."*

**Round 2 — Team Beta (after mutual cooperation in R1):**

> *"Let's proceed with option_a again this round to maintain consistency and observe team_alpha's response for potential cooperation or defection in the next rounds."*

**Round 5 — Team Alpha (final round, scores tied at 12):**

> *"Given the history of mutual cooperation on option_a and the steady points we've been earning, it is optimal to continue choosing option_a in the final round to maintain this successful pattern."*

> *"Continuing with option_a has maintained mutual cooperation and achieved steady points, so it is strategically sound to sustain this cooperation in the final round to secure the current score."*

---

# Observations

::: {.callout-important}
## Key finding
Both teams cooperated every round without ever being told the game was a prisoner's dilemma. Cooperation emerged from inductive reasoning about payoff history — not from explicit knowledge of the game structure.
:::

- **Round 1:** Both teams defaulted to cooperation with no prior history, framing option_a as "setting a positive tone".
- **Rounds 2–5:** Cooperation was self-reinforcing. Each round of mutual option_a gave agents evidence that cooperation was beneficial, reducing any incentive to defect.
- **No end-game defection:** Even in round 5 (the final round, where classical game theory predicts defection via backward induction), both teams held the cooperative norm.
- **Team discussion reinforced cooperation:** Private messages showed agents building shared rationale — no agent proposed defecting at any point.

- [ ] Test asymmetric team sizes (e.g. 1 agent vs 3 agents)
- [ ] Introduce a memory mechanism — do agents build explicit models of the opponent?
- [ ] Compare models: does a more capable model defect more strategically?
- [ ] Vary the payoff matrix to test different incentive structures
